questions.q: What does the .data directive tell the assembler and linker?
choices: Everything after it is executable code for the text segment
Everything after it is data to be placed in the data segment of memory
Everything after it is allocated on the stack at runtime
Everything after it is ignored, like a comment
questions.explain: .text marks executable code for the text/code segment. .data marks data that goes into the data segment.

questions.q: A program with only a .text section is still using RAM, because its code is loaded into the text (code) segment of memory.
questions.explain: The code itself lives in RAM. In the emulator the text segment starts at 0x401000 and the data segment at 0x402000.

questions.q: In the data section, what does a name followed by a colon (for example r16:) do?
choices: Declares a new CPU register named r16
Creates a label that refers to the memory address where the data after it begins
questions.explain: Like _start:, a label is a name for an address. The name r16 is just a name. It is not a register, and it does not set a size.

questions.q: Each memory address refers to a single byte.
questions.explain: An 8-byte value starting at 0x402000 takes up addresses 0x402000 through 0x402007.

questions.q: To read the data stored right after the r17 label, you have to use the name r17. There is no other way to reach those bytes.
questions.explain: Labels are just a convenience. If r16 is at 0x402000 and holds an 8-byte quad, the next data starts at 0x402008. You can get there by adding 8 to r16's address.

questions.q: How many bytes are in a quadword?
questions.explain: A word is 2 bytes. A double word is 2 words (4 bytes). A quadword is 4 words (8 bytes).

questions.q: On x86-64, how many bytes are in a 'word'?
questions.explain: On x86-64 a word is 16 bits, which is 2 bytes.

questions.q: In the GNU assembler, which directive declares a 4-byte (double word, 32-bit) value?
questions.explain: In the GNU assembler a 4-byte double word is written as .long.

questions.q: Which list gives the sizes in bytes of .byte, .word, .long, and .quad, in that order?
questions.explain: .byte = 1, .word = 2, .long = 4 (double word), .quad = 8 (quadword).

questions.q: How many hexadecimal digits does it take to write out a full 8-byte value?
questions.explain: Two hex digits make one byte, so 8 bytes need 16 hex digits.

questions.category: Loading from memory: mov vs lea
questions.q: The label r16 is at address 0x402000 and holds .quad 0xAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA. One instruction does a mov from the memory operand r16 (label in parentheses) into RAX. Another does lea of r16 into RBX. What do RAX and RBX hold afterward?
questions.explain: mov with a memory operand copies the data stored at the address. lea (load effective address) copies the address itself.

questions.category: Loading from memory: mov vs lea
questions.q: What do parentheses (brackets) around a label or register in a mov operand mean?
choices: Use the value as a literal number to copy
Use the value as a memory address and access the data stored there
Compute the address but don't access memory
Mark the operand as a 4-byte value
questions.explain: The brackets turn the operand into a memory access: go to that address and read (or write) the data there.

questions.category: Loading from memory: mov vs lea
questions.q: What is the mnemonic of the 'load effective address' instruction?
questions.explain: lea puts an address into a register without reading the memory at that address.

questions.category: Loading from memory: mov vs lea
questions.q: A label was declared with .quad. You mov from that address into a register. What decides how many bytes are read?
choices: The directive used to declare the data (.quad means 8 bytes are always read)
The size of the destination register
The distance to the next label
Nothing: it is always exactly 1 byte, because one address holds one byte
questions.explain: The register doesn't know how the data was declared. RAX asks for 8 bytes, EAX for 4, AX for 2, and AL for 1.

questions.category: Loading from memory: mov vs lea
questions.q: Loading from a .quad label into AL reads all 8 bytes, because the data was declared as a quadword.
questions.explain: AL is a 1-byte register, so it reads only the single byte at that address (the least significant byte of the quad).

questions.q: Which of these are parts (subsets) of the RAX register?
questions.explain: EAX is the low 4 bytes of RAX. AX is the low 2 bytes of EAX. AH and AL are the high and low bytes of AX. RBX is a separate register.

questions.q: Which register is the 2-byte subset of RAX?
questions.explain: RAX = 8 bytes, EAX = 4, AX = 2, and AH/AL = 1 each.

questions.q: RAX holds 0x1122334455667788. What value is in AH?
questions.explain: AX is the low 2 bytes (0x7788). AH is the high byte of AX (0x77) and AL is the low byte (0x88).

questions.q: RAX holds 0x1122334455667788. What value is in EAX? (hex)
questions.explain: EAX is the lower 4 bytes of RAX.

questions.q: .quad 0x0123456789ABCDEF is stored starting at address 0x402000. Which byte is at 0x402000? (hex)
questions.explain: Multi-byte values are stored least significant byte first, so memory holds EF CD AB 89 67 45 23 01.

questions.q: Same data: .quad 0x0123456789ABCDEF at 0x402000. Which byte is at 0x402007? (hex)
questions.explain: The most significant byte goes at the highest address of the 8.

questions.q: .quad 0x0123456789ABCDEF is at 0x402000. You load from 0x402000 into EAX. What does EAX hold?
questions.explain: EAX reads 4 bytes (EF CD AB 89) and puts them back together least significant first, giving the lower half of the value.

questions.q: Same data, but this time you load from 0x402000 into AX. What does AX hold?
questions.explain: AX reads the 2 bytes EF CD, which make the value 0xCDEF.

questions.q: A label is followed by .word 0xABCD. In what order are the two bytes stored, from lower address to higher?
questions.explain: The least significant byte (CD) is written first, then AB. Each byte stays the same; only the byte order is reversed.

questions.q: memory: .byte 0x01, 0x02, 0x03, 0x04. You load from the address of memory into EAX. What does EAX hold?
questions.explain: The byte at the lowest address (01) becomes the least significant byte, so the four bytes make 0x04030201. It works like a type cast.

questions.q: Same data (.byte 0x01, 0x02, 0x03, 0x04), but loaded into AX. What does AX hold?
questions.explain: AX reads only the first two bytes (01 02), which make 0x0201.

questions.q: RAX holds the address 0x402000. How do you make it point to the next 8 bytes?
questions.explain: Each address is one byte, so moving 8 bytes forward means adding 8 (0x402000 becomes 0x402008).

questions.q: Starting at 0x402000, memory holds r16: .quad 0x0123456789ABCDEF, followed by r17: .quad 0xBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBB. You put the address of r16 in RAX, add 4, then load 8 bytes from the address in RAX into RBX. What is in RBX?
questions.explain: The bytes from 0x402004 are 67 45 23 01 BB BB BB BB. Read least significant first, they make 0xBBBBBBBB01234567. RBX takes 8 bytes no matter where the labels are.

questions.q: Adding 8 to a register that holds a memory address, then reading through it, is like incrementing a pointer in C.
questions.explain: The register works as a memory pointer. Changing it changes which memory you access.

questions.q: A memory layout covers every byte from 0x402000 through 0x40201A, inclusive. How many bytes is that?
questions.explain: 0x1A = 26, and counting both ends gives 27 bytes: three 8-byte quads (24) plus 3 bytes.

questions.q: RAX = 0x123456 and RBX = 0x402000 (the memory there is zeroed). You store RAX to the memory address in RBX. Which bytes end up at 0x402000 through 0x402007?
questions.explain: RAX always writes 8 bytes, least significant first. The upper bytes of the value are zero, so zeros are written too.

questions.q: Storing a small value such as 0x123456 from RAX to memory still writes 8 bytes, and the upper bytes are written as zeros.
questions.explain: The size of the write is the size of the register. RAX writes 8 bytes even when most of them are zero.

questions.q: How many bytes are written to memory when you store EAX to an address?
questions.explain: EAX is a 4-byte (double word) register.

questions.q: Memory at 0x402000..0x402007 must hold exactly these bytes: 13 D7 C0 FF 02 5A 37 00. Which .quad value produces this layout?
questions.explain: Read the bytes from the highest address down to the lowest: 00 37 5A 02 FF C0 D7 13. The leading 00 can be left out.

questions.q: .quad 0xA4CDCE6BE1935500 is stored at 0x402008. Which byte is at 0x402009? (hex)
questions.explain: The bytes stored are 00 55 93 E1 6B CE CD A4, so 0x402008 holds 00 and 0x402009 holds 55.

questions.q: The last part of a layout must be the bytes 1A 1A 1A. If you write .long 0x1A1A1A, what ends up in memory?
questions.explain: There is no 3-byte size, so a 4-byte .long is used. The value's top byte is 00, and it is stored last.

questions.q: RSI points to where you want to write single bytes from AL, one after another. What do you do between byte writes?
questions.explain: Each byte has its own address, so the pointer moves forward by 1 for each byte (for example with inc).

questions.q: Moving a value into AL also clears the rest of RAX to zero.
questions.explain: Writing to AL, AH, or AX changes only those bytes. The rest of RAX keeps its old contents.

questions.q: Moving a value into EAX zeroes the upper 4 bytes of RAX.
questions.explain: Writing EAX is the exception: it automatically zeroes the upper half of RAX.

questions.q: RAX holds 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF. You move 0x1A into AL. What does RAX hold now?
questions.explain: Only the lowest byte (AL) changes. The other 7 bytes keep their old value.

questions.q: Which of these writes leave the other bytes of RAX unchanged?
questions.explain: AL, AH, and AX change only their own bytes. A write to EAX zeroes the upper 4 bytes of RAX.

questions.q: Which of these set all of RAX to zero?
choices: Move the immediate value 0 into RAX
questions.explain: Moving 0 into RAX works, and XOR-ing RAX with itself is the more efficient way. Writing 0 to AL or AX clears only those bytes.

questions.q: What does .skip 1024, 0xFF do in the data section?
questions.explain: .skip (or .space) takes a byte count and an optional fill value for every byte.

questions.q: Which GNU assembler directives allocate a given number of bytes (optionally filled with a value) without listing each value?
questions.explain: .space and .skip reserve a block of a given size. .byte needs every value written out, and .text starts the code section.

questions.q: Data-segment space allocated without a fill value starts out as zeros.
questions.explain: Memory is zeroed by default. That is why the leftover bytes after a write show up as 00 unless you choose a fill such as 0xFF.
